==Problem==

A line that passes through the origin intersects both the line <math> x = 1</math> and the line <math>y=1+ \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} x</math>. The three lines create an equilateral triangle. What is the perimeter of the triangle?

<math> \textbf{(A)}\ 2\sqrt{6} \qquad\textbf{(B)} \ 2+2\sqrt{3} \qquad\textbf{(C)} \ 6 \qquad\textbf{(D)} \ 3 + 2\sqrt{3} \qquad\textbf{(E)} \ 6 + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} </math>

==Solution 1==

Since the triangle is equilateral and one of the sides is a vertical line, the triangle must have a horizontal line of symmetry, and therefore the other two sides will have opposite slopes. The slope of the other given line is <imath>\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}</imath> (which is must be, given 60 degree angle of the triangle, relative to vertical) so the third must be <imath>-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}</imath>. Since this third line passes through the origin, its equation is simply <imath>y = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}x</imath>. To find two vertices of the triangle, plug in <imath>x=1</imath> to both the other equations. 

<imath>y = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}</imath>

<imath>y = 1 + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}</imath>

We now have the coordinates of two vertices, <imath>\left(1, -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\right)</imath> and <imath>\left(1, 1 + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\right)</imath>. The length of one side is the distance between the y-coordinates, or <imath>1 +  \frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}</imath>.

The perimeter of the triangle is thus <imath>3\left(1 +  \frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\right)</imath>, so the answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D) }3 + 2\sqrt{3}}</imath>

Note: We know that the slope for the third line must be <imath>-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}</imath>, as the slope for the second given line is <imath>\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}</imath>. The slope is determined from two points on a line, and we pick one of the points to be the point where they intersect. Now, drawing the symmetric line, it splits the first line; x=1 into two equal parts. Now, the second point for the third and second lines have the same x coordinate, but opposite y coordinates.

===Solution 1 Different Approach===

It is important to note that because \( \tan(x) \) represents the slope of a function, then \( \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} \) is just \( \tan(30^\circ) \). Then, if we reflect \( \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} x+1 \) over the line \( y=\frac{1}{2} \), we get \( y=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}x \) as our new function.

Given that, we may resume with solution 1.

==Solution 2==
Draw a line from the y-intercept of the equation  <math>y=1+ \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} x</math> perpendicular to the line <math>x=1</math>. There is a square of side length 1 inscribed in the equilateral triangle. The problem becomes reduced to finding the perimeter of an equilateral triangle with a square of side length 1 inscribed in it. The side length is <math>2\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) + 1</math>. After multiplying the side length by 3 and rationalizing, you get <math>\boxed{\textbf{(D) }3 + 2\sqrt{3}}</math>.

==Solution 3==
Let the intersection point between the line <imath>y = 1 + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}x</imath> and the line that crosses the origin be <imath>P</imath>.

We drop an altitude from <imath>P</imath> onto the line <imath>x = 1</imath>. Since the overall triangle is an equilateral triangle, we are splitting the base (on <imath>x=1</imath>) in half. As the y-axis is parallel to the line <imath>x=1</imath>, the altitude from P will also split the y-axis from <imath>y=0</imath> to <imath>y=1</imath> in half. From this, we can get that the y-value of P is <imath>\frac{1}{2}</imath>.

Plugging this into the equation <imath>y = 1 + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}x</imath>, we get that <imath>x = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}</imath>, and thus our height for the equilateral triangle is <imath>1 + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}</imath>. Using that, we can calculate the perimeter to be <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D) }3 + 2\sqrt{3}}</imath>.

==Solution 4 (quick)==
<imath>1+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}x</imath> clearly must form a 60 degree angle with <imath>x=1</imath>. The other line is the one that forms a <imath>-60</imath> degree angle with <imath>x=1</imath>. Thus, it must have slope <imath>-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}</imath>, and equation <imath>y-0=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}(x-0)</imath>.

This equation, <imath>x=1</imath>, and the x-axis form a 30-60-90 triangle. The length of the short leg is <imath>0-(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}(1))</imath> or <imath>\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}</imath>. Multiplying by 2 gives the hypotenuse and then by 3 gives the perimeter, <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D) }3 + 2\sqrt{3}}</imath>

==Solution 5 (coord bash)==
Suppose that the line is <imath>y=kx</imath>. The intersections of lines <imath>y=kx</imath> and <imath>x=1</imath>, <imath>y=kx</imath> and <imath>y=1+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}x</imath>, <imath>x=1</imath> and <imath>y=1+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}x</imath>, are <imath>(1,k),\quad \left(\dfrac{3}{3k-\sqrt{3}},\dfrac{3k}{3k-\sqrt{3}}\right),\quad \left(1,\dfrac{3+\sqrt{3}}{3}\right)</imath> respectively. Because these 3 points form an equilateral triangle, the distances between these points are equal. Therefore, we get the equation <imath>\left(\dfrac{3}{3k-\sqrt{3}}-1\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{3k}{3k-\sqrt{3}}-k\right)^2=\left(\dfrac{3+\sqrt{3}}{3}-k\right)^2</imath>. Then by re-writing every term as a single fraction, we get <imath>\left(\dfrac{3-3k+\sqrt{3}}{3k-\sqrt{3}}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{3k-3k^2+\sqrt{3}\,k}{3k-\sqrt{3}}\right)^2=\left(\dfrac{3+\sqrt{3}-3k}{3}\right)^2</imath>.
Then we can factor out <imath>3+\sqrt{3}-3k</imath> from every term, which gets us
<imath>(3+\sqrt{3}-3k)\cdot\dfrac{(3+\sqrt{3}-3k)(1+k^2)}{(3k-\sqrt{3})^2}=(3+\sqrt{3}-3k)\cdot\dfrac{3+\sqrt{3}-3k}{9}</imath>.
Cancelling out <imath>3+\sqrt{3}-3k</imath> gets us <imath>\dfrac{1+k^2}{(3k-\sqrt{3})^2}=\dfrac{1}{9}</imath>. Solving this equation gets us

\begin{gather*}
9(1+k^2) = (3k-\sqrt{3})^2 \\[6pt]
9+9k^2 = 9k^2 - 6\sqrt{3}\,k + 3 \\[6pt]
9 = -6\sqrt{3}\,k + 3 \\[6pt]
6 = -6\sqrt{3}\,k \\[6pt]
k = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}
\end{gather*}
Now we can find the perimeter of the equilateral triangle. Using the distance between <imath>\left(1,\dfrac{3+\sqrt{3}}{3}\right)</imath> and <imath>(1,k)</imath>, the side length of the equilateral triangle is <imath>1+\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}-\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\right) = 1+\dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}</imath>. Therefore, the perimeter of the triangle is <imath>3\left(1+\dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\right) = 3 + 2\sqrt{3}</imath>, which gives us the answer <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D) }3 + 2\sqrt{3}}</imath>
